967: The region that immediately draws attention on a map of Gujarat through its geographical vastness and distinctive shape is Kutch. Spread over 45,674 square kilometres, this land is not only Gujarat's largest district but, after Ladakh, the second largest in all of India by area. Kutch, whose geographical size dwarfs even entire states such as Haryana or Kerala, is more than a piece of land. It is a supreme example of the earth's geological upheavals, the glory of the Indus Valley Civilization, the sensitivity of international maritime boundaries, and the human will to create something from nothing.
970: Geologically, Kutch falls in Seismic Zone 5. Fault lines beneath the earth here, such as the Kutch Mainland Fault (KMF), Katrol Hill Fault and Island Belt Fault, make this region extremely vulnerable to earthquakes. The devastating earthquake of 1819 changed the course of the Indus River and raised the ground by 6 metres, a formation historians call the Allah Bund. The earthquake of 26 January 2001 was one of the greatest natural disasters in modern Indian history.
972: Kutch's historical heritage is five thousand years old. Dholavira, on Khadir Bet, is India's largest Indus Valley Civilization site and the 40th UNESCO World Heritage Site. This ancient city is famous for its three-tier urban planning, enormous stone structures and the world's oldest water-harvesting system. When the world was in the early stages of civilization, Dholavira already possessed the engineering skill to collect every drop of rainwater in reservoirs.
974: Mandvi port's history was so illustrious that a fleet of around 400 ships anchored here in the 18th century. The 400-year-old craft of building wooden ships on the banks of Mandvi's Rukmavati River remains alive today, and ships built here sail as far as the Gulf countries.
975: Kutch's economic transformation after the 2001 earthquake is a case study in modern economics. The economic policies announced by the government of the time and infrastructure development established Kutch among the country's leading industrial centres.
978: Salt: India is the world's third-largest salt producer, and Gujarat accounts for more than 75% of India's total salt production, with the lion's share coming from Kutch's coast and the Little Rann.
979: Mineral Wealth: Kutch is rich in lignite, bauxite, bentonite and china clay. India's premium bentonite is exported from Kutch to countries around the world.
981: Kutch's true soul resides in its folk arts and handicrafts. A local saying goes, 'The land in Kutch may be dry, but the hearts of its people and their needles and threads are full of colour.'
983: Ajrakh Printing (Ajrakhpur): This art of printing on both sides of fabric with wooden blocks, using natural dyes such as indigo, pomegranate rind and turmeric, has links to the time of the Indus Civilization.
984: Kutchi Embroidery: The intricate mirror-and-thread embroidery made by women of the Ahir, Rabari, Mutwa and Jat communities inspires global fashion designers today.
986: Culturally, the Kutchi New Year is celebrated on Ashadhi Bij, a day associated with hopes for the arrival of rain. The Ravechi fair, Haji Pir fair and festivals of the Jagir region offer a glimpse of Kutch's communal harmony and its tradition of Sufis and saints.
988: In the 18th and 19th centuries, the Kutchi Bhatia, Kutchi Lohana, Kutchi Jain and Kutchi Memon communities travelled to places such as Muscat, Zanzibar, Mombasa, Kenya and Uganda in East Africa and established trading empires. Today, Kutchi merchants have left an indelible mark on markets considered the backbone of Mumbai's economy, such as its textile, grain and metal markets. The Kutchi diaspora spread across the UK, the United States and the Gulf countries maintains a deep bond with its birthplace. Whenever natural disaster has struck Kutch, this global diaspora has revived its homeland by sending billions of rupees in donations and aid.
992: Strategic and Defence Importance: Kutch's western boundary adjoins Pakistan. The 96-kilometre stretch of water at Sir Creek and Harami Nala are extremely sensitive from the standpoint of national security. Personnel of the Indian Army, Air Force and the Border Security Force's (BSF) Water Wing defend the country's borders with extraordinary courage in this difficult marshland.
994: From the ancient engineers of Dholavira to the modern engineers installing solar panels at Khavda... from Mandvi's seafarers to Mundra's global traders... Kutch has proved that it is possible to reach the heights of modernity while preserving one's heritage. This is steadfast, unbowed and timeless Kutch, through all twelve months!
1014:
[Part 2: Ancient History and the Indus Civilization - The Port of Lothal]
Ahmedabad's history is not merely 600 years old. If we look back thousands of years, we find Lothal in the Bhal region of Ahmedabad district. This Indus Valley Civilization town had the world's oldest and first tidal dockyard, a port governed by the ebb and flow of the tides. Its engineers had such remarkable knowledge of sea tides and water currents that they could bring ships directly into the town. Today, the Government of India is building the National Maritime Heritage Complex here.
1015: Later, in the 11th century, this area was known as Ashaval. King Karnadeva of the Chaulukya dynasty conquered it and established the city of Karnavati. Then came the moment in 1411 when Gujarat's Sultan Ahmad Shah saw a hare attack a dog on the banks of the Sabarmati, and on this courageous land the foundations of present-day Ahmedabad were laid.
1018:
[Part 4: The Epicentre of the Indian Freedom Struggle]
Whenever the history of India's struggle for independence is written, Ahmedabad's name will be inscribed in golden letters. When Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915, he made Ahmedabad his field of work: first Kochrab Ashram, and then Sabarmati Ashram. This is the very land from which the historic Dandi March began in 1930, shaking the foundations of the British Empire.
1020:
[Part 5: Economy - From the 'Manchester of India' to an 'Auto and Pharma Hub']
Trade runs in Gujaratis' blood, and Ahmedabad is its capital. In 1861, Ranchhodlal Chhotalal opened the first cotton textile mill here, the Gujarat Spinning and Weaving Company. Soon mill sirens began sounding across Ahmedabad, and the British gave it the title 'Manchester of India'.
1022: The Sanand industrial area proved a game changer. In 2008, when the Tata Nano plant was moved out of Singur in West Bengal, Gujarat welcomed it to Sanand. Today, companies such as Tata, Ford (now owned by Tata), Maruti and Panasonic have created such a large automobile hub in Sanand that it is on its way to becoming the 'Detroit of India'. Bhaliya wheat, grown in the Bhal region and bearing a Geographical Indication (GI) tag, is another jewel in the local agricultural economy.
1025:
[Part 7: Culture, Food and Festivals]
Ahmedabad is more than a money-making machine; this city knows how to live. Its Navratri is the world's longest-running dance festival. On Uttarayan, all of Ahmedabad is on its rooftops and the sky is covered with kites. The International Kite Festival is now a global tourism event.
1027:
[Part 8: Vision 2047 - A Future Metropolis and Sports Capital]
What does Ahmedabad's future look like? The Sabarmati River, which had once dried into something like a puddle, was filled with Narmada water to create the Sabarmati Riverfront model, which has now become an urban development concept for other cities throughout the country.
1029:
[Conclusion]
Ahmedabad is not merely a city made of bricks and cement. It is an idea that combines the glory of the past with soaring aspirations for the future. The Ahmedabadi who discusses global trade while sitting on a pol's front platform knows how to absorb change. The journey that began at Lothal's port has now reached ISRO's satellites. This is Ahmedabad: Gujarat's heart, India's growth engine and the living heritage of centuries.
1044:
District: Amreli (The Land of Braves and Bountiful Nature)
Part 1: Introduction - A Unique Union of Courage and Nature
Amreli... a district beating in the heart of Saurashtra that has made invaluable contributions to Gujarat's history, literature and politics. From the natural beauty of Gir's forests, every corner of this sacred land of saints and heroes tells stories of courage and resilience. It is also known as a land of writers, having given Gujarat literary greats such as Kalapi and Ramesh Parekh. Amreli may seem geographically small, but its social and cultural stature is immense.
A distinctive enthusiasm and energy can be found in every particle of this district. Amreli is not simply a geographical place but a living experience. Even the dust of its villages carries the fragrance of hard work and honesty. The murmuring waters of its rivers and its chains of hills give the region a unique identity. Such a beautiful balance between nature and human life is rarely found elsewhere. The spirited pride of Amreli's people and their belief in treating a guest as God charm every visitor.
1046:
Part 3: Geography and Ecology - Nature's Remarkable Treasure
Amreli district is geographically diverse. On one side are Gir's dense forests, and on the other are vast farms and plains. Amreli is one of the few Gujarat districts that directly benefit from Gir National Park. The roar of Asiatic lions is often heard in its forest areas, an extraordinary experience for wildlife lovers. Dhari and Khambha talukas lie within the Gir forest boundary, where leopards, nilgai, chinkara and many kinds of birds can be seen.
Rivers such as the Shetrunji, Shingavdo and Dhatarwadi are Amreli district's lifelines. They provide water not only for farming but also for wildlife. Khodiyar Dam on the Shetrunji meets the area's principal irrigation and drinking-water needs. During the monsoon, these rivers and the dam become picturesque, with greenery all around. The district's climate is generally dry and hot, but winter brings a gentle chill.
Gir's ecology extends beyond lions; a great treasure of medicinal plants is hidden here too. Amreli's farmers and pastoralists have learned the art of living in coexistence with nature. Local people are conscious of wildlife conservation and participate in government efforts. As the geographical conditions also favour wind and solar power, renewable-energy projects are gradually taking shape here.
1048:
Part 5: Culture and Everyday Life - A Heritage of Pride and Resilience
Amreli's culture is an excellent example of Kathiawadi culture. Its people are simple-hearted yet proud. The traditions of Kathi Darbars and other communities are still visible in social life. Saurashtra's renowned folk literature, dayro performances and lively devotional singing form part of daily village life. Echoes of couplets, metrical verse and Charani literature continually resonate here. An Amreli feast is special too, with sev-and-tomato curry, pearl millet rotla, olo and traditional jaggery and ghee.
Janmashtami, Navratri and Diwali are celebrated with great enthusiasm. The folk fairs held especially during Shravan are a true expression of Amreli's rural life. Watching traditional raas-garba and sword raas at social celebrations and weddings is a delight. Local artisans are skilled in Kathiawadi embroidery, beadwork and patchwork. The decorative torans and embroidered square hangings made by village women are popular in India and abroad.
This land of saints and spiritual leaders has numerous religious sites that are centres of faith. Sant Muldas, Bhoja Bhagat and many other saints spread devotion and knowledge from this soil. Hundreds of thousands of devotees visit nearby pilgrimage sites such as Chalala and Bagdana to bow in reverence. People's lives are simple, yet their thoughts remain profound and hospitality always lives in their hearts. This folk life of Amreli is a living symbol of Gujarat's identity.
1050:
Conclusion
Amreli district is not merely a part of Saurashtra; it is the heart of Gujarat's strength, culture and prosperity. From poet Kalapi's verses to the roar of Gir's lions, and from Savarkundla's weighing scales to cotton swaying in the fields, Amreli has much to offer the world. Its glorious history and its people's hard work always make it distinctive and remarkable.
As Amreli climbs new steps of development, it holds ever more firmly to its roots. A hundred salutes to this land where courage, literature and nature meet like three sacred rivers. Amreli's journey teaches us that true progress is one in which tradition and modernity walk shoulder to shoulder.
1064:
Part 2: Historical Heritage - Charotar's Pride and the Freedom Struggle
Anand and the surrounding Charotar region have an exceptionally rich history. The contribution of Charotar's Patidars and other farming communities to India's independence movement is inscribed in golden letters. During the Kheda and Borsad satyagrahas under Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Anand district remained a major centre of national awakening. Karamsad, Sardar Patel's hometown, lies in this district. This land gave us an Iron Man like Sardar, who performed the great task of binding the entire country together.
Anand's historical heritage is educational as well as political. Behind Vidyanagar's establishment was the vision of Bhaikaka (Bhikhabhai Patel) and Bhikhabhai, who transformed barren land into Gujarat's largest educational hub. Sardar Patel University and many other prestigious educational institutions have made this area a city of knowledge. Khambhat, formerly known as Stambhatirth, was an exceptionally busy and prosperous port in ancient times, trading spices and silk with every corner of the world.
Thus, Anand's history is not merely one of kings and princely states, but of people's strength, their hunger for education and their spirit of cooperation. The seeds planted by its freedom fighters, educators and visionaries now stand as an enormous, fruitful banyan tree, providing shelter and employment to hundreds of thousands.
1066:
Part 4: Economy and Industry - The Dairy Industry and Global Exports
Dairy and farming are the mainstays of Anand district's economy. Amul Dairy (Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union Limited), India's largest food brand, is based in Anand. The dairy processes hundreds of thousands of litres of milk daily and makes products including butter, cheese, powder, chocolate and ice cream for export worldwide. This cooperative model gives farmers a fair price directly for their milk, greatly strengthening the rural economy.
In agriculture, tobacco production and processing factories make an important economic contribution. Elecon, an elevator manufacturer in Anand's Vidyanagar industrial area, is also a leader across Asia in manufacturing gears and material-handling equipment. Khambhat is world-famous for its agate industry. Beautiful jewellery and artworks made here from agate stones are in great demand abroad. Khambhat's locks and kites are also very well known.
Food-processing, pharmaceutical and engineering industries have established a presence in Anand. National institutions such as the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) and the Institute of Rural Management Anand (IRMA) are based here and undertake foundational work in agriculture and rural management. The educational and medical hubs of Vallabh Vidyanagar and Karamsad attract large numbers of students and patients, keeping the local economy active.
1068:
Part 6: Vision 2047 and Modern Infrastructure - Towards a Smart and Global City
Under Vision 2047, ambitious plans are being implemented to develop Anand district as an educational, agro-industrial and smart city. A major station on the Ahmedabad–Mumbai bullet train project (high-speed rail) is being built in Anand. This station will increase Anand's connectivity and commercial possibilities tenfold. The proximity to Mumbai and Ahmedabad provided by the bullet train will make Anand a future economic hub. Renovation of the expressway and other state highways is bringing a major transformation in logistics.
In agriculture, artificial intelligence (AI) and automation have begun to be used to modernize the dairy industry further. Smart collars and IoT-based systems are being introduced to track animal health. In education too, institutions such as CHARUSAT and CVM University are becoming research centres of global standards.
For clean energy and a green environment, rooftop solar panels and biogas plants are being installed throughout Anand district on a large scale. Under NDDB's 'Sudridh' biogas project, an initiative has begun to produce bio-CNG from cattle dung, which will prove a game changer in renewable energy in the future. By 2047, Anand is set to become India's most exemplary smart-rural and educational capital.
1084:
Part 2: Historical Heritage - Shamlaji and the Remains of Buddhist Culture
Aravalli district's history is thousands of years old. Shamlaji Temple is an extremely important Vaishnav pilgrimage site not only for Gujarat but for all of western India. This ancient temple on the Meshwo River is an outstanding example of architectural art. The black-marble image of Lord Shamlaji enshrined here is a symbol of supreme faith for devotees. The temple's history is believed to extend to the Gupta period.
Archaeological excavations in the district's Devni Mori area also attracted historians from across India. Buddhist stupas and Buddha statues from the third or fourth century were found here, proving Buddhism's great influence in this region in ancient times. The Buddha's bone relics found here testify to Gujarat's glorious Buddhist heritage.
Under Rajput rulers and the Mughal Empire too, the region was strategically very important because it lay on the main route connecting Gujarat and Delhi. Old forts and ruins around Modasa and Bhiloda witnessed wars and political intrigue. Tribal revolts against British rule are also an inseparable part of this region's history, reflecting its people's yearning for freedom.
1086:
Part 4: Economy and Industry - A New Centre of Farming and Trade
Aravalli district's economy is primarily agricultural. Farming takes place on a large scale in talukas such as Modasa, Malpur and Meghraj. Wheat, maize, groundnuts, cotton and soybeans are the main crops. The construction of canals and check dams has improved irrigation, enabling farmers to grow more than one crop. Alongside farming, animal husbandry is an important income source. With Sabar Dairy's support, milk production has increased considerably.
Industrially, Modasa is developing as a major transport and automobile hub. Its truck- and bus-body manufacturing industry is highly developed and known throughout India. Local craftspeople are so skilled that commercial-vehicle body orders come even from neighbouring states. Textiles, agro-processing and small engineering units are also boosting the district's economy. GIDC estates are creating new employment opportunities for local youth.
1088:
Part 6: Vision 2047 and Modern Infrastructure - Balancing Progress and the Environment
Under Vision 2047, Aravalli district is ready to develop as an ecotourism and logistics hub. Construction of the Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) and other national highways is rapidly increasing commercial activity in Modasa and surrounding areas. Modernization of the road network has given the region direct connections to all of northern India.
Education and healthcare facilities in tribal areas are being significantly improved. Eklavya Model Residential Schools provide advanced education to tribal children in remote areas. An ambitious plan is taking shape for an international heritage and spiritual tourism circuit linking the Devni Mori Buddhist stupa and Shamlaji. Work is underway towards a Buddhist theme park and meditation centre here that will attract visitors from around the world.
Organic farming is being encouraged so that Aravalli's farmers can obtain good prices in national markets. Drones and digital monitoring are being used for wildlife and forest conservation. In the future, Aravalli will enhance Gujarat's pride as a sustainable heritage tourism hub, beyond its identity as a remote district.
1102:
District: Banaskantha (The Land of Agriculture and Divine Blessings)
Part 1: Introduction - A Land of Shaktipeeth and Agricultural Revolution
Banaskantha... Gujarat's northernmost district, with the state's largest geographical area. Once a dry, semi-desert region bordering Rajasthan's desert, it has now become Gujarat's largest agricultural producer. Its hardworking farmers, cooperative dairy industry and Mother Amba's blessings have played a major role in this transformation.
Situated on the banks of the Banas River, this district is at the heart of Gujarat's culture and faith. Here the Aravalli ranges meet desert sands in a remarkable confluence. Mother Amba, enshrined on Gabbar hill, is the focus of faith for hundreds of thousands of devotees. Whether through Palanpur's royal, perfume-scented history or Deesa's potato production, Banaskantha is leaving its distinctive mark in every field. This land has proved that hard work, even under difficult conditions, can make roses bloom in the desert.
1104:
Part 3: Geography and Ecology - A Journey from Desert Sands to Greenery
Banaskantha's geography is extremely varied: Aravalli hills in the north, the Little Rann of Kutch in the west, and the fertile Banas River plain in the centre. The Banas, Sipu and Balaram are its main rivers, remaining mostly dry outside the monsoon. Dantiwada and Sipu dams are the district's lifelines and have transformed agriculture. The arrival of the Narmada Canal brought a green revolution to Banaskantha, making even dry areas cultivable.
Banaskantha is ecologically very rich. Balaram–Ambaji Wildlife Sanctuary and Jessore Sloth Bear Sanctuary are paradises for nature lovers. Jessore's forests shelter bears, leopards, wild boar and numerous bird species. In contrast, Nadabet and Suigam have desert ecology, with wild asses and desert foxes. The climate is highly extreme, marked by intense summer heat and bone-chilling winter cold.
1106:
Part 5: Culture and Everyday Life - Faith, Devotion and Tribal Colours
Banaskantha's everyday life is colourful and filled with religious festivals. Ambaji hosts the great Bhadarvi Poonam fair, where hundreds of thousands of pilgrims arrive on foot, raising resounding cries of 'Call out to Mother Amba, victory to Mother Amba'. Witnessing this surge of faith is an extraordinary experience. The people here are deeply devout and hardworking.
Tribal culture predominates in Danta and Amirgadh talukas. The Garasia and Bhil communities still preserve their ancient dance traditions and customs. Embroidery and pottery play a major part in Banaskantha's folk arts. Mirror embroidery and Kutchi work by Ahir and Rabari women in Radhanpur and Vav are especially famous. The staple food is pearl millet rotla, traditional butter, jaggery and kadhi, which replenish the body's energy on cold days. Raas and garba performed to drumbeats at social occasions provide a distinctive attraction.
1108:
Conclusion
Banaskantha is Gujarat's greatest story of determination and transformation. The people of this region, once thirsty for every drop of water, have combined hard work and technology to make even the desert green. Mother Amba's boundless grace and the farmers' sweat together make golden crops sway on this land.
The air carries the fragrance of perfume and the soil the scent of hard work. Banaskantha's unceasing journey of development shows that when leadership, cooperation and people's willpower come together, anything impossible can be made possible. In the coming years, Banaskantha will remain a role model in agriculture and cooperation for all of India.
1123:
Part 2: Historical Heritage - The Glorious Journey from Bhrigukachchha to Bharuch
Bharuch's history is as old as the Puranas. It is believed that Maharishi Bhrigu founded this city, giving it the name Bhrigukachchha. Greek and Roman travellers knew it as Barygaza. From before the Common Era through the medieval period, Bharuch was western India's largest international port. Spices, cotton textiles, silk and many valuable goods were exported from here to the Roman Empire and Arab countries.
Bharuch retained its economic and political importance during the Solanki era, the Sultanate period and Mughal rule. Later, the Dutch and British East India Companies also established trading posts here. Even today, the Dutch cemetery and old British-era buildings in Bharuch testify to this European influence. Writers and revolutionaries such as Kanhaiyalal Munshi enhanced Bharuch's honour in the freedom struggle. The Golden Bridge, built by the British across the Narmada, remains a symbol of Bharuch's engineering heritage and a principal city landmark.
1125:
Part 4: Economy and Industry - India's Chemical and Petrochemical Hub
Bharuch's true identity lies in its immense industrial development. Ankleshwar Industrial Estate is Asia's largest chemical GIDC, housing hundreds of chemical, pharmaceutical and dye factories. ONGC (Oil and Natural Gas Corporation) extracts crude oil and natural gas here on a large scale. Jhagadia, Panoli and Valia also have large industrial parks where tyre, glass and engineering companies have invested billions of rupees.
Dahej has developed as a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and a Petroleum, Chemicals and Petrochemicals Investment Region (PCPIR). Adani Port and Reliance Industries' large plants in Dahej contribute immensely to India's economy. This industrialization has attracted job seekers from every corner of the country, turning Bharuch into a mini-India. Alongside industry, bumper cotton crops in the Kanam region and banana production strongly support Bharuch's agricultural economy. Bharuch's salted peanuts are famous nationwide and widely traded.
1127:
Part 6: Vision 2047 and Modern Infrastructure - A Global Industrial Smart City
With Vision 2047, Bharuch is on its way to becoming the country's smartest industrial and logistics hub. The Delhi–Mumbai Expressway and Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC) projects are giving Bharuch world-class connectivity. A bullet train station is also taking shape in Bharuch, which will connect it to Mumbai and Ahmedabad at superfast speeds. Expansion of Dahej Port and waterway connections to Saurashtra through the Ro-Ro ferry service are revolutionizing transport.
For environmentally friendly development, Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) technology is being made compulsory in industrial areas. New green hydrogen and biochemical plant projects are being established in Dahej, helping make Bharuch a carbon-neutral industrial zone. Smart traffic management, riverfront development and modern residential townships in urban areas are transforming Bharuch into an advanced 21st-century metropolis.
1141:
District: Bhavnagar (The Land of Bravery and Enterprise)
[Part 1: Introduction - Saurashtra's Cultural Capital]
Bhavnagar district, on Gujarat's eastern coast beside the Gulf of Khambhat, is a remarkable meeting of culture, literature, courage and sculpture. Known as Saurashtra's cultural capital, this city is renowned worldwide for its glorious history and distinct identity. Bhavnagar is more than a district: it is a living tradition where modernity and antiquity walk shoulder to shoulder. Poets' verses and saints' words echo in its air.
1143: Whenever Gujarat's literature or education is discussed, Bhavnagar's name is always prominent. Great educators such as Gijubhai Badheka and Nanabhai Bhatt lit a unique flame of learning on this very soil. The district's people are exceptionally affectionate and hospitable. Bhavnagar is moving towards becoming a smart city that embraces future technology while preserving its historical heritage. Come, let us explore this remarkable district in depth and discover all its aspects.
1145: Maharaja Krishnakumarsinhji is an exceptionally important and respected name in Bhavnagar's history. After Indian independence, he was the first ruler to dedicate everything he possessed to the nation in response to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's call for integration. His sacrifice and patriotism still inspire every Indian. Bhavnagar princely state was also known throughout India for its progressive administration, interest in education and public welfare work. Its rulers encouraged girls' education and founded many educational institutions.
1147:
[Part 3: Geography and Ecology - The Gulf of Khambhat Coast and Velavadar]
Bhavnagar district is geographically diverse. The Gulf of Khambhat lies to its east, giving it a long, strategic coastline. This coast has enabled the development of numerous ports and maritime industries. Bhavnagar's climate ranges mostly from temperate to hot and dry. Winter weather is very pleasant, while summer brings some heat. The Shetrunji is the most important of the region's rivers and serves as the district's lifeline. Shetrunji Dam, built across it, is extremely important for irrigation and drinking water.
1149: Mangrove forests also occur along the coast and are vital to environmental balance. Mahuva taluka is known as the 'Kashmir of Saurashtra' for its greenery and fertile soil. Its vast coconut groves create a picturesque coastal landscape. A small island called Piram Bet near Bhavnagar is known for its biodiversity and ancient fossils. Thus, Bhavnagar's geography and ecology are highly diverse and attract nature lovers.
1151: Bhavnagar district is making notable progress in agriculture too. Its main crops include groundnuts, cotton, onions and pearl millet. Mahuva is known throughout India for its red onions, which are also exported on a large scale. Numerous onion-dehydration plants here make onion powder and flakes for overseas markets. Mahuva's coconuts and guavas are also very popular. Irrigation made possible by Shetrunji Dam has significantly increased agricultural production.
1153:
[Part 5: Culture and Everyday Life - Folk Literature and Delicious Gathiya]
Bhavnagar's culture is a remarkable confluence of art, literature, music and taste. Everyday life here is very simple yet rooted in deep cultural values. Bhavnagar has always been celebrated as Gujarat's cultural capital. Its people's love of art is unmatched. In literature, the district has inspired Ravishankar Raval, Dula Bhaya Kag and many other great creators. Bhavnagar's dayro performances and devotional music evenings are famous throughout Gujarat. The region also contributed greatly to national poet Jhaverchand Meghani's research into folk literature.
1155: In food, Bhavnagar and gathiya have become synonymous. Bhavnagari gathiya are famous not only in Gujarat but throughout India and abroad. People travel long distances to eat the local puffs, bread with gathiya and various sweets. The people are very sociable and affectionate. An evening stroll along Bor Lake and a chat with friends are a delightful part of Bhavnagar's everyday life. The spirit of treating guests as God resides in every corner, making any visitor feel part of Bhavnagar.
1157: Bhavnagar Port is being modernized. A new CNG terminal is under construction and will become the world's first CNG port terminal. This project will develop Bhavnagar into a major logistics hub and create many new jobs. Bhavnagar will also directly benefit from its proximity to Dholera Smart City (Dholera SIR). Dholera–Bhavnagar expressway and rail-connectivity projects are progressing rapidly, connecting the district's industries more quickly to global markets.
1159:
[Conclusion]
Bhavnagar district is more than a part of Gujarat; it is Saurashtra's heart. Its journey from a glorious history to the development of modern ports is deeply inspiring. While Velavadar's blackbuck convey an environmental message, Alang's shipyard conveys economic strength. Narsinh Mehta's morning hymns and Maharaja Krishnakumarsinhji's sacrifice testify to this land's greatness.
1173:
District: Botad (The Land of Spirituality and Cotton)
[Part 1: Introduction - A New Home of Faith and Prosperity]
Botad district, a gateway to Saurashtra on Gujarat's map, is a unique centre of faith, enterprise and tradition. Created in 2013 from parts of Bhavnagar and Ahmedabad districts, this new district is now making great leaps in development. Botad is a land where spirituality flows continuously and economic prosperity grows from cotton fields. Geographically and culturally, it connects the boundaries of Bhal and Gohilwad.
1176:
[Part 2: Historical Heritage - Kathiawad's Tales of Courage]
Botad's history is full of heroic tales of Kathi Darbars and princely states. In ancient times, this region was an inseparable part of Kathiawad. Kathi rulers dominated here in the 18th and 19th centuries. Many battles were fought on Botad's soil and many heroes sacrificed their lives. In time, the area came under Bhavnagar princely state's rule. Bhavnagar's rulers contributed significantly to Botad's development, including laying railway lines and encouraging trade.
1178: National poet Jhaverchand Meghani spent much of his life in Botad. Many heroic stories he recounted in 'Saurashtra ni Rasdhar' are connected to surrounding areas. Botad's people also played an active role in the independence movement. Local youth participated in large numbers in Gandhiji's Non-Cooperation Movement and the Dandi March. Botad's historical heritage thus resembles a confluence of religion, literature and courage that still inspires new generations.
1180: The main rivers here include the Ghela, Kalubhar and Sukhbhadar. The Ghela flows past Gadhada and has great religious as well as geographical importance. The Sukhbhadar is useful for irrigation, and dams built across it are a blessing for Botad. However, low groundwater levels have made water conservation an important issue here.
1182:
[Part 4: Economy and Industry - Ginning Mills and the Diamond Industry]
Botad's economy is mainly based on agriculture and related industries. As cotton is the main crop, Botad city is a vast centre of cotton ginning and pressing. Numerous mills separate cotton fibre and press it into bales. Groundnuts, sesame, pearl millet and sorghum are also cultivated on a large scale. Botad's Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) is considered one of Gujarat's largest and most active markets.
1184: Small and medium enterprises, including textiles, oil mills and transport, also strengthen the economy. As Botad is a railway junction, rail transport is well developed and extremely useful for moving goods and conducting trade. In recent years, agro-processing and food-packaging industries have also begun establishing themselves here, creating more employment opportunities in the future.
1186: Literature and music are integral to everyday life here. Folk literature has developed extensively under Jhaverchand Meghani's influence. Festivals such as Navratri and Janmashtami resound with garba and folk dayro performances. Saurashtra's traditions of saints' songs and bhajans remain alive in Botad's villages. People gather to sing devotional songs and preserve their cultural heritage.
1187: Kathiawadi cuisine dominates local food. Pearl millet rotla, mashed roasted aubergine, sev-and-tomato curry and buttermilk are staples. Sweets such as lapsi and mohanthal are prepared for festivals. Botad's people may seem somewhat stern, but at heart they are extremely loving and generous. Hospitality runs in their blood. All these things make Botad culturally very rich.
1189: To address water shortages, efforts to deliver Narmada water to Botad's reservoirs under the SAUNI Yojana are being strengthened. In the future, special emphasis will be placed on water storage and micro-irrigation to increase production through drop-by-drop farming. Farmers are also being encouraged to produce solar energy so they can become energy providers as well as food providers.
1191:
[Conclusion]
Botad district is a remarkable combination of labour, faith and literature. This land where Jhaverchand Meghani worked still keeps the same pride and courage alive. The blessings of Salangpur Dada and the farmers' hard work continually lead the district towards progress. The sparkle of diamonds and cotton's white revolution have made Botad economically strong.
1205:
District: Chhota Udepur (The Land of Tribal Heritage and Minerals)
[Part 1: Introduction - The Heart of Tribal Culture]
On Gujarat's eastern edge beside the Madhya Pradesh border, Chhota Udepur district is a remarkable jewel of natural beauty and tribal culture. Created in 2013 by separating from Vadodara district, it is one of Gujarat's most attractive forest-covered regions. Chhota Udepur beautifully combines lush forests, murmuring rivers and vibrant tribal life. Forest fragrances mingle with the notes of tribal folk songs in its air.
1207: Today, Chhota Udepur is progressing rapidly in education, health and infrastructure. Once considered backward, this area is now reaching new heights of development. Rich in mineral resources, the district also contributes greatly to Gujarat's economy. Come, let us explore this picturesque, culturally rich district in depth and discover its unique heritage.
1209: Chhota Udepur city still offers glimpses of princely-era grandeur. Kusum Vilas Palace and Prem Bhavan Palace are incomparable architectural examples. These palaces beautifully blend European and Indian architectural styles. Kusum Vilas Palace's grand gates, fountains and carvings especially mesmerize visitors. These rulers were great patrons of art and culture, whose influence is still visible in Chhota Udepur today.
1211:
[Part 3: Geography and Ecology - Forests and the Orsang River]
Chhota Udepur's geography is exceptionally attractive and varied. The district is mainly hilly and forest-covered. The outer reaches of the Vindhya Range lie here, creating hills of varying sizes and valleys. During the monsoon, the entire region wears a green blanket, with scenery that could rival any hill station. The climate is generally hot and humid, but the forests make nights pleasant.
1213: The district is very rich in ecology and wildlife. Teak, mahua, timru, khakhra and bamboo grow abundantly in its forests. Mahua is like a wish-fulfilling tree for tribal people: its flowers and fruits form a large part of their daily life and economy. Leopards, wild boar, monkeys and various birds inhabit these forests. Local people's bond with nature is so unbreakable that they worship trees and rivers, an excellent example of environmental conservation.
1215: Local farmers mainly grow maize, pigeon peas, soybeans, cotton and groundnuts. The Orsang River and various check dams have improved irrigation. However, a large section still relies on rain-fed agriculture. Pastoralists also practise animal husbandry alongside farming, supporting the rural economy.
1217:
[Part 5: Culture and Everyday Life - Pithora Art and the Kavant Fair]
Chhota Udepur's culture is a living heartbeat of colour, music, dance and festivals. Its tribal communities have proudly preserved their distinctive identity. Pithora painting is the area's greatest cultural heritage. These paintings are more than art: for the Rathwa community, they are a means of worshipping their revered deity, Baba Pithora. Horses, elephants, deities and natural scenes are painted on house walls with natural colours. This art has received worldwide recognition.
1219: The food here is simple. Maize rotla, black gram dal, wild greens and a drink made from mahua are staples. People are extremely simple, candid and hardworking. With education spreading today, young people have turned towards modernity but have not forgotten their cultural values. Chhota Udepur's culture offers an excellent example of living in harmony with nature.
1221: New ITIs and vocational training centres are being established for tribal youth's skill development so they can build careers in industry and services. Plans aim to connect Pithora painting and bamboo crafts to e-commerce platforms and global markets, ensuring craftspeople receive fair prices for their work.
1222: In infrastructure, expansion of the broad-gauge railway will connect Chhota Udepur more firmly with other parts of the country. New, wider highways are being built to make mineral-industry transport faster and safer. In healthcare, a modern civil hospital and health and wellness centres in every village are operational. Renewable-energy and water-management projects will make Chhota Udepur a sustainable, self-reliant district by 2047.
1237:
District: Dahod (The Land of Rising Sun and Tribal Legacy)
[Part 1: Introduction - Gujarat's First Sunrise]
Dahod district on Gujarat's eastern border is a source of pride for the state. Its name comes from 'Do-had', or two boundaries, because it borders the two states of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. The district is geographically and culturally very important. Gujarat's first sunrise occurs in Dahod district, so it is also called Gujarat's 'Sunrise City'. Formed in 1997 by separating from Panchmahal district, it is now writing new chapters in education, health and development.
1240:
[Part 2: Historical Heritage - Aurangzeb's Birth and the Bhil Kings]
Dahod's historical heritage is magnificent and fascinating. The region is believed to have been known in ancient times as the place where Sage Dadhichi performed penance. Bhil kings ruled Dahod for a long period, undertaking many works for its security and prosperity. The heroes of this land fiercely resisted foreign invaders and made sacrifices to preserve their independence.
1242: Dahod's tribal people actively participated in the independence movement. They made great sacrifices in rebellions against the British and in the Forest Satyagraha. Inspired by Mahatma Gandhi and Sardar Patel, numerous activities for tribal advancement began in Dahod, with especially important contributions from social workers such as Thakkar Bapa and Pujya Mota. Dahod's history is thus a collection of remarkable stories of kings, Mughal emperors and freedom fighters.
1244: Dahod district holds a distinctive place in Gujarat for ecology and wildlife. Ratanmahal Sloth Bear Sanctuary here is one of India's best protected areas for bears. The sanctuary is rich in diverse vegetation, dense teak forests and medicinal plants. Besides bears, it shelters leopards, wild boar, monkeys, nilgai and many kinds of birds.
1245: During the monsoon, Ratanmahal looks no less beautiful than a hill station. Its forests are a principal source of livelihood for tribal people, providing produce such as timru leaves, honey, lac and gum. Canals from Kadana and Panam dams irrigate some areas, helping bring a green revolution even to this mountainous landscape.
1247: Industrially, Dahod Railway Workshop is very well known. Established in 1912 during British rule, it is an extremely important Western Railway centre. Railway locomotives and coaches are repaired here. Recently, the Government of India approved a factory here to manufacture advanced 9,000-horsepower (HP) electric locomotives. This Rs 20,000-crore project under 'Make in India' will transform Dahod's economy and create thousands of new jobs.
1249:
[Part 5: Culture and Everyday Life - Bhil Tribals and the Gol Gadheda Fair]
Dahod's culture is a supreme example of harmony between nature and human life. Its Bhil tribal culture is known for its festivals, dances and clothing. Holi and Navratri are celebrated with tremendous enthusiasm. During Holi, the atmosphere resounds with drumbeats. Jesawada's Gol Gadheda fair, held after Holi, is especially famous. Young men compete to climb a tall pole and retrieve a bundle of jaggery while women try to stop them with bamboo sticks. It is an exceptionally exciting traditional festival.
1252:
[Part 6: Vision 2047 and Modern Infrastructure - Smart City and Electric Locomotive Factory]
Dahod is Gujarat's only tribal city selected under the Government of India's Smart City Mission. Under Vision 2047, its infrastructure is undergoing fundamental changes. Chhab Lake has been renovated and developed into a grand tourist destination and city centre. A modern CCTV network, Wi-Fi zones, smart traffic management and clean drinking-water facilities have been provided in the city.
1254: In education, a new medical college and engineering colleges have been established under Govind Guru University, allowing tribal youth to obtain higher education close to home. In healthcare, Zydus Medical College and Hospital provides modern facilities. Dahod of the future will be a fully digital, industrially developed city that preserves tribal traditions.
1269:
District: Dang (The Land of Pristine Forests and Tribals)
[Part 1: Introduction - Gujarat's Cherrapunji and Nature's Embrace]
Dang district, on Gujarat's southern edge beside the Maharashtra border, is a true natural paradise. Though Gujarat's smallest district in population and area, its natural beauty and cultural richness are immense. Its climate, dense forests and murmuring streams have earned it the names 'Gujarat's Cherrapunji' and 'Gujarat's Kashmir'.
1271: Today, Dang extends beyond tourism: it has become India's first district practising 100% organic farming. Once considered extremely backward, this region now sends a global message of environmental and health preservation. Come, let us explore this small yet remarkable district in depth.
1273: In modern history, Dang's tribal kings never accepted complete subjugation, even during British rule. There were five principal states here: Gadhvi, Daher, Linga, Pipri and Vasurna. Numerous conflicts occurred between these Bhil kings and the British. Finally, in 1842, the British and Dang's kings signed a treaty concerning forest rights. To commemorate it, the British started the Dang Darbar, where the kings received an annual allowance or pension.
1274: After independence, the Government of India continued this tradition. Even today, the Dang Darbar is held in Ahwa a few days before Holi, welcoming all five kings with full royal honours. Dang is the only district in India where the Government of India still pays pensions to former rulers. Thus, Dang's history, from the Ramayana era to today's democracy, has been exceptionally interesting and unique.
1276: Ecologically, Dang is Gujarat's largest forest area. Purna Wildlife Sanctuary and Vansda National Park (on the Navsari border) are treasures of biodiversity. These forests contain large bamboo, teak, haldarvo and salai trees. Bamboo forests in particular define Dang. Wildlife includes leopards, wild boar, deer, chital and rare species such as the flying squirrel.
1278:
[Part 4: Economy and Industry - 100% Organic Farming and Forest Produce]
Dang district has no large factories or industries, and perhaps that is its greatest strength. Its economy depends entirely on agriculture, animal husbandry, tourism and forest produce. A few years ago, the Gujarat government declared Dang the state's first district practising 100% natural (organic) farming. Farmers avoid chemical fertilizers and pesticides, cultivating with cow dung, cow urine and jeevamrit.
1280: Tourism is the largest pillar of Dang's economy. Thousands visit places such as Saputara, Shabari Dham, Don Hill Station and Mahal Campsite, providing employment for local hotels, guides and traders. Homestays are also developing, allowing tourists to stay in tribal homes and experience their culture. Dang's economy is thus developing without harming nature.
1282: Warli painting is also widespread in Dang. People paint beautiful white geometric shapes on the walls of their mud houses, depicting scenes of farming and forest life. Dungar Dev and Vagh Dev are worshipped during festivals. Local faith is rooted in the elements of nature.
1284:
[Part 6: Vision 2047 and Modern Infrastructure - A Global Ecotourism Hub]
Dang has every potential to emerge as a model ecotourism and organic district in building a Developed India by 2047. The state government's vision is to make Dang a global tourism hub while preserving its natural balance. In addition to Saputara, Don is being developed as a new hill station, offering tourists new destinations.
1286: To encourage organic farming, agro-processing units are planned here so produce such as finger millet and honey can be exported directly to international markets. Telemedicine and renewable energy are helping Dang's remote villages become self-reliant. Dang in 2047 will be a living example of the best combination of environmental care and modernity.
1288: Today, while the whole world suffers from global warming and pollution, Dang shows us the right path to environmental preservation. Its remarkable heritage and intimate bond with nature are an invaluable gift to future generations. Heartfelt wishes that the beauty of Dang, this sacred meeting of nature and culture, remains intact forever and that it reaches the heights of progress!
1303: When we speak of Devbhumi Dwarka, a golden city comes to mind, believed to have been built by Shri Krishna and submerged in the sea. Even today, archaeologists find remains of that ancient city on the seabed, lending reality to this mythological story. The district came into existence on 15 August 2013, separated from Gujarat's Jamnagar district. Khambhalia, the district headquarters, is famous worldwide for ghee and sweets. Dwarka city on the Gomti River gives pilgrims an extraordinary sense of peace.
1304: Devbhumi Dwarka brings devotion and strength together in a remarkable way. When Jagat Mandir's 52-yard flag flies in the wind, every devotee's heart fills with Krishna. Meanwhile, Bet Dwarka island, Shivrajpur's Blue Flag beach and beautiful coastal views mesmerize visitors. Nature has scattered beauty generously here, and culture has coloured it with faith. Come, let us journey through this sacred land's history, geography, economy, culture and future to understand why Devbhumi Dwarka matters so much to Gujarat and India.
1306: In ancient times, Dwarka and its surroundings were known as Okhamandal. Under the Maurya, Gupta and Maitraka dynasties, this area was an important port and trading centre. The original foundations of the present Dwarkadhish temple, known as Jagat Mandir, are believed to have been laid by Shri Krishna's great-grandson Vajranabh. The current magnificent seven-storey, 78-metre-high temple was built in the 15th–16th centuries in the Chaulukya style. During Islamic invasions, particularly by Mahmud Begada, the area was attacked and temples damaged. Yet the local people's unshakable faith and periodic restorations have kept this sacred shrine standing.
1308: After independence, the region became part of Saurashtra state in 1947, then the larger Bombay state, and finally Gujarat in 1960. After decades as part of Jamnagar district, Devbhumi Dwarka received separate district status in 2013 under then Chief Minister Shri Narendra Modi to improve administration and accelerate local development. Today, the district is taking firm steps towards modernity while preserving its glorious historical heritage.
1310: Geographically and ecologically, Devbhumi Dwarka is a paradise of marine biodiversity. Part of the Marine National Park and Sanctuary in the Gulf of Kutch touches the district, sheltering coral reefs, varied marine vegetation and rare aquatic life. Coastal mangroves serve as breeding grounds for marine creatures and play an important role in environmental balance. Large numbers of migratory birds arrive in winter, attracting bird lovers. Flamingos, pelicans and cranes are especially seen in the Charakla salt pans and around Mithapur.
1312:
[Part 4: Economy and Industry - Development Based on Agriculture, Minerals and Tourism]
Devbhumi Dwarka district's economy mainly depends on farming, animal husbandry, fishing, mineral industries and tourism. Despite saline coastal soils, farming is substantial inland. Groundnuts, cotton, pearl millet, wheat, sesame and castor are the main crops. Khambhalia, Bhanvad and Kalyanpur talukas lead in agriculture. Animal husbandry is also the backbone of the rural economy. 'Khambhalia's pure ghee' is so famous across Gujarat that it has become synonymous with purity and flavour. Alongside Gir and Kankrej cows, Jaffarabadi buffaloes are found in large numbers.
1314: Mineral resources contribute greatly to Devbhumi Dwarka's economy. Its abundant bauxite and limestone reserves provide crucial raw materials for the cement industry. However, tourism is the district's fastest-growing economic sector. Hundreds of thousands of devotees and tourists visit Dwarka, Bet Dwarka, Nageshwar Jyotirlinga, Rukmini Temple, Gomti Ghat and Shivrajpur Beach each year. This influx has brought substantial growth in hotels, transport, handicraft sales and local employment. Tourism has become a thriving year-round industry rather than merely a seasonal business.
1316: Janmashtami is the most important festival here. Dwarka's Janmashtami fair and celebrations are famous throughout India, not just Gujarat. The devotional atmosphere at Jagat Mandir at the moment of Krishna's birth is difficult to describe. A special Phuldol festival is also celebrated during Holi-Dhuleti, when hundreds of thousands of pilgrims walk to see Dwarkadhish. Rath Yatra, Shivratri (especially at Nageshwar Jyotirlinga) and Navratri are also celebrated enthusiastically. Khichdi and kadhi offered as prasad have special significance at Bet Dwarka.
1318:
[Part 6: Vision 2047 and Modern Infrastructure - A New Flight of Development]
Devbhumi Dwarka is moving rapidly towards the future with the vision of 'Developed India 2047', alongside its glorious past. The central and state governments have undertaken major projects to equip the district with modern infrastructure. The most important is Sudarshan Setu (Signature Bridge), connecting Okha and Bet Dwarka. Previously, Bet Dwarka could only be reached by boat, but this modern 2.32-kilometre cable-stayed bridge has made access much easier for tourists and residents. Its solar panels and Bhagavad Gita verses make it an outstanding example of modernity and spirituality together.
1320: The district is also making great strides in renewable energy. With conditions favourable for wind and solar power, numerous windmills and solar parks have been established. Under the Digital India Mission, rural areas are being connected by optical fibre so e-governance, education and healthcare can reach even the most remote residents. A new civil hospital and medical college will be a major blessing for the district's youth and patients. Under Vision 2047, efforts to make Devbhumi Dwarka a global spiritual and tourism hub are gathering pace.
1335: District: Gandhinagar (The Green Capital of Gujarat)
1336:
[Part 1: Introduction - A Green Capital Born from a Dream]
Gandhinagar is not only Gujarat's capital but a city exemplifying modern Indian urbanization. On the western bank of the Sabarmati River, it is famous nationwide for its peaceful atmosphere, broad roads and abundant greenery. Named after Mahatma Gandhi, the Father of the Nation, it is independent India's second entirely planned city after Chandigarh. When Gujarat and Maharashtra separated from Bombay state in 1960, Gujarat needed a new capital, and this beautiful city was born.
